title: Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
context: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterized by high blood glucose levels resulting from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. It is the most common form of diabetes, accounting for 90-95% of all diabetes cases. Risk factors include obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, and age over 45 years. Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, increased hunger, fatigue, and blurred vision. Management involves lifestyle modifications such as diet and exercise, along with medications like metformin, sulfonylureas, and insulin when necessary.

title: Hypertension Pathophysiology
context: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg. It is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and kidney disease. The pathophysiology involves increased peripheral vascular resistance, increased cardiac output, or both. Contributing factors include increased sympathetic nervous system activity, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, and endothelial dysfunction. Treatment includes lifestyle modifications and antihypertensive medications such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics.

title: Acute Myocardial Infarction
context: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), commonly known as a heart attack, occurs when blood flow to a part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a blood clot in a coronary artery. This leads to ischemia and potentially irreversible myocardial damage. Symptoms include chest pain or discomfort, shortness of breath, nausea, and sweating. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, ECG changes (ST-segment elevation or depression), and elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin I or T). Immediate treatment includes aspirin, antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and reperfusion therapy via percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or thrombolysis.

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
context: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive lung disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation. The main causes are cigarette smoking and long-term exposure to air pollutants. COPD includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. Spirometry showing FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70 confirms the diagnosis. Management involves smoking cessation, bronchodilators (beta-agonists and anticholinergics), inhaled corticosteroids for severe cases, pulmonary rehabilitation, and oxygen therapy for hypoxemic patients.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
context: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease primarily affecting the joints. It is characterized by symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, and joint swelling. The disease can also affect extra-articular organs. Diagnosis involves clinical criteria, elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and positive rheumatoid factor (RF) or anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA). Treatment includes disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate, biologic agents (TNF inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors), and NSAIDs for symptomatic relief.

title: Hypothyroidism
context: Hypothyroidism is a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce sufficient thyroid hormones. The most common cause in iodine-sufficient areas is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition. Symptoms include fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and depression. Laboratory findings show elevated TSH and low free T4 levels. Treatment involves levothyroxine replacement therapy, with dose adjusted based on TSH levels. Patients require lifelong treatment and regular monitoring.

title: Pneumonia Clinical Features
context: Pneumonia is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Common bacterial pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical organisms like Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Clinical features include fever, cough with purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnea. Physical examination may reveal crackles and bronchial breath sounds. Chest X-ray typically shows consolidation. Treatment depends on severity and includes antibiotics such as beta-lactams, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones.

title: Acute Kidney Injury
context: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as a sudden decrease in kidney function occurring over hours to days. It is diagnosed by elevated serum creatinine, decreased urine output, or both. Causes are categorized as prerenal (hypoperfusion), intrinsic renal (glomerular, tubular, or interstitial damage), or postrenal (obstruction). Management involves treating the underlying cause, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, avoiding nephrotoxic agents, and providing renal replacement therapy if needed for severe cases.

title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
context: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition where stomach acid frequently flows back into the esophagus, causing irritation. Common symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, and chronic cough. Risk factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, and certain foods or medications. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, though endoscopy may be performed for complications or atypical symptoms. Treatment includes lifestyle modifications (weight loss, avoiding trigger foods), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), H2 receptor antagonists, and antacids.

title: Alzheimer's Disease
context: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia. It is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain. Early symptoms include memory loss, especially of recent events, and difficulty with problem-solving. As the disease progresses, patients experience confusion, disorientation, behavioral changes, and difficulty speaking or swallowing. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by cognitive testing and brain imaging (MRI or PET). Treatment includes cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) and NMDA receptor antagonists (memantine) to slow symptom progression.
